title: ‘Among many I go first’
theme: Alone, the boy reflects on his worth and wonders what Death could want with him.

words.context: Śaṅkara: first, in the best conduct among pupils or sons

words.meaning: purpose, what is to be done

sandhi.rule: A final m before a vowel stays m and joins the next word.
aḥ becomes o before a voiced consonant, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च).
A final t before m becomes n, P. 8.4.45 (यरोऽनुनासिकेऽनुनासिको वा); mayā + adya → mayādya, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः).

morphology.note: Gerundive of kṛ, ‘what is to be done’, used as a noun: ‘purpose, business’. Śaṅkara glosses it as prayojana.
An interrogative particle adding doubt: kiṃ svit, ‘what, I wonder?’

translation.literal: Among many I go first; among many I go in the middle. What, I wonder, is Yama’s purpose, which he will accomplish with me today?
translation.readable: ‘Among many I go first, among many in the middle. What could Yama want with me, that he will do today?’

anvaya: [अहम्] बहूनाम् प्रथमः एमि, बहूनाम् मध्यमः एमि । यमस्य किम् स्वित् कर्तव्यम् [अस्ति] यत् [सः] अद्य मया करिष्यति ॥
syntax: Two parallel statements (‘among many I go first / in the middle’) and a question with a relative clause. The speaker is the boy, alone; the verse is a soliloquy.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: among many pupils or sons I conduct myself as the best or at least the middling, never the worst — the boy reflects on his worth. Raṅgarāmānuja: among all who go to Death’s house I go at the front or in the middle, not behind — I am not afraid. The words allow both.
Śaṅkara calls it a lament in private (paridevana). Raṅgarāmānuja says the boy spoke ‘free of fear and grief’ («विगतसाध्वसशोकः»), and only wondered what use a child could be to Death.

beginner: The boy has been given to Death in a moment of anger. Alone, he thinks it over. ‘Among many I go first; among many I go in the middle.’ The commentators read this in two ways. One: he has always been a good son and pupil, among the best or at least the average, never the worst, so why should he be thrown away? The other: whenever people go to Death, he will be at the front or in the middle, not hanging back, because he is not afraid. Then he asks: what could Death want with me? He does not argue with his father’s words. He takes them as something that must now happen, and wonders what it will mean.
analogy: Like a soldier who, ordered somewhere unexpectedly, does not protest but asks quietly what he could possibly be needed for there.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: The boy says that among many he goes first or in the middle, and asks what Yama’s purpose could be that he will accomplish with him today.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: alone, the son lamented — «स एवमुक्तः पुत्रः एकान्ते परिदेवयाञ्चकार». He concludes that his father spoke in anger, not with any purpose — «नूनं प्रयोजनमनपेक्ष्यैव क्रोधवशादुक्तवान् पिता» — yet resolves that the father’s word must not be made false: «तथापि तत्पितुर्वचो मृषा मा भूदिति».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: As fearlessness: «सर्वेषां मृत्युसदनगन्तृणां पुरतो मध्ये वा गच्छामि» — among all who go to Death’s house I go in front or in the middle. What troubles him is only his own use: «पूर्णकामस्य मृत्योः मादृशेन बालिशेन किं प्रयोजनं स्यात्», what purpose could Death, who wants nothing, have for a child like me?

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Madhva’s bhāṣya has no separate comment on this mantra; the verse he cites for 1.1.5–7 begins with the boy’s journey: «स जगाम यमं बालो ब्रह्मचारी यमस्य तु».

advaita.text: A lament in private that ends in resolve: the father’s word must stand — «तथापि तत्पितुर्वचो मृषा मा भूदिति».

visistadvaita.text: Not a lament but fearless reflection: the boy goes first or in the middle among those who go to Death, and wonders only what use he could be: «पूर्णकामस्य मृत्योः मादृशेन बालिशेन किं प्रयोजनं स्यात्».

schools.disagreement: Śaṅkara hears a lament, Raṅgarāmānuja calm courage. Both readings are possible from the words; neither changes the outcome.

contemporary.text: When someone we depend on treats us carelessly, we can protest, or we can ask what the new situation requires of us. The boy does the second. This is a modern reflection, not the text’s claim.

reflect.beginner: When things go badly for you because of someone else, what is your first thought?
reflect.deeper: Is it possible to accept a situation without accepting that it was right?
reflect.practice: Think of one difficult situation you are in and ask, as the boy does, what it might be for.

flags.note: Two readings of the first line: the boy’s worth among pupils and sons (Śaṅkara) or his place among those who go to Death (Raṅgarāmānuja).
